To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a RIG-I ligand (5′pppppppppppRNA) is an efficient inhibitor of DENV and CHIVK replication, both in vitro and in vivo.

the stimulation of RIG-I with an optimized 5’pppRNA molecule before or after infection generates a protective antivirals response against both DENV and CHKV in human primary immune and nonimmune cell types.

RIG-I stimulation with 5′pppppppRNA before infection or postinfection with DENV or with CHIKV generates a potent antiviral response and that this response was dependent on an unimpaired RIG-I/MDA5/MAVS/Tbk1/IRF-3 pathway.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery of novel antiviral agents against emerging viruses, which are difficult to diagnose, and for which no therapeutic agents exist.
the identification of new therapeutic strategies against DENV and Chikunguna virus infections.
the identification of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of viral infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of RIG-I stimulation as a therapy to treat DENV or CHIVK infection would be an interesting approach to pursue.
the RIG-I/5′ppp RNA agonist combination may be an effective therapeutic strategy against both DENV and CHIVK infections.

this study demonstrates that RIG-I agonism is an effective antiviral strategy for DENV and CHKIV, and that the protective effect of the RIG-I activator is independent of the type-1 interferon response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the RIG-I ligand 5′pppppRNA can be used to treat DENV and CHIVK infections.

the use of 5′-pppRNA as an adjuvant in vaccines against these emerging viruses would likely improve the immune response against them, as well as provide an additional layer of protection against infection.
RIG-I activation is sufficient for the induction of an antiviral state against DENV and that this antiviral state is independent of the type 1 interferon response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RIG-I agonism may be a promising therapeutic option for the treatment of emerging RNA virus infections.
the innate immune response is a potential target to treat viral infections.
the RIG-I/MDA5 agonists may have therapeutic potential against DENV and other arbovirus infections, and that the antiviral activity of these compounds is independent of the type 1 IFN response.
